title: Amplitude Modulation
description: AM waveforms, sidebands and power, suppressed-carrier and single-sideband signals, and how they are generated and detected.

study.title: Explore: the AM waveform
study.body: The message is added to the carrier amplitude: the outline of the waveform, the **envelope**, is a copy of the modulating signal. The **modulation index** $m = V_m/V_c$ (×100 % = percentage modulation) must stay between 0 and 1. Drag $m$ past 1: the envelope (dashed) crosses zero and the waveform no longer follows it. This **overmodulation** distorts the detected audio and creates extra sidebands (splatter) that interfere with neighbouring channels.

study.title: Modulation index from the envelope
study.body: On an oscilloscope, read the envelope peak $V_{max}$ and the envelope trough $V_{min}$ (both peak values, or both peak-to-peak). Then $V_c = (V_{max} + V_{min})/2$ and $V_m = (V_{max} - V_{min})/2$, so the index follows without knowing the carrier separately. $V_{min} = 0$ means exactly 100 % modulation.

study.title: Explore: sidebands and bandwidth
study.body: Multiplying out the AM equation gives three sinusoids: the unchanged carrier at $f_c$ and two **side frequencies** at $f_c \pm f_m$, each with amplitude $mV_c/2$. A band of audio frequencies up to $f_{m,max}$ gives a lower and an upper **sideband**, so the bandwidth is $2f_{m,max}$: 9–10 kHz for AM broadcast, 6 kHz for 3 kHz speech. The sketch uses $f_c$ = 1 MHz and $f_m$ = 5 kHz; drag $m$: the carrier never changes, only the sidebands grow.

readouts.label: share of total power in the sidebands

study.title: AM power
study.body: Power goes with amplitude squared, so each sideband carries $(m/2)^2 = m^2/4$ of the carrier power and the total is $P_c(1 + m^2/2)$. Even at $m = 1$ the sidebands, which carry all the information, get only one third of the total; with speech the average share is much lower. The antenna current rises to $I_T = I_c\sqrt{1 + m^2/2}$, which is a simple way to measure $m$.

study.title: DSB-SC, SSB and VSB
study.body: A **balanced modulator** suppresses the carrier and leaves both sidebands (**DSB-SC**). Removing one sideband as well gives **SSB**: half the bandwidth and all power in the information, but the receiver must re-insert a carrier of the right frequency. SSB with speech has a varying envelope, rated by its **peak envelope power** (PEP); the average power of speech is only about PEP/3 to PEP/4. **VSB** keeps one sideband plus a vestige of the other (analog TV video, ATSC 8-VSB).

study.title: Modulators and SSB generation
study.body: AM is a multiplication: the carrier times $(1 + m\,x(t))$. **Low-level** modulators (diode, transistor, analog multiplier) make AM at small power, followed by linear amplifiers; **high-level** modulation varies the supply of the class C final stage (collector modulation). A **balanced modulator** multiplies message and carrier, leaving only sum and difference frequencies. SSB then comes from the **filter method** (a steep crystal filter removes one sideband) or the **phasing method** (two balanced modulators fed with 90°-shifted carrier and audio; subtracting their outputs cancels one sideband).
study.formula: v_m \times v_c \;\Rightarrow\; f_c - f_m,\ f_c + f_m

study.title: Explore: the envelope detector
study.body: A diode charges $C$ to each carrier peak and $R$ discharges it in between, so the output (red) follows the envelope. $RC$ must be long compared with a carrier period (small ripple) but short enough to follow the falling envelope; if not, the output decays slower than the envelope: **diagonal clipping** (Frenzel: diagonal distortion). Here $f_c = 40f_m$. DSB-SC and SSB have no usable envelope and need **synchronous detection**: multiply by a local carrier of the same frequency and phase (product detector), then low-pass filter.

steps.title: Amplitude modulation
steps.body: In AM the message changes the **amplitude** of a carrier: the carrier peak becomes $V_c + v_m(t)$. For a tone $v_m = V_m\sin\omega_m t$, the outline of the waveform (the **envelope**, dashed) is a copy of the tone. The ratio $m = V_m/V_c$ is the **modulation index**; this sketch has $m$ = 0.5.

steps.prompt: A carrier of {{Vc|V}} peak is amplitude-modulated by a tone of {{Vm|V}} peak.

ask.prompt: Find the modulation index $m$.
Find the percentage of modulation.

steps.title: m from the envelope
steps.body: On a scope you rarely see $V_c$ and $V_m$ separately. Read the largest envelope value $V_{max}$ and the smallest $V_{min}$: the carrier is their average and the tone amplitude half their difference.

steps.prompt: The scope is zoomed in on the upper half of an AM trace. Read $V_{max}$ and $V_{min}$ of the envelope and find the modulation index.
steps.explanation:
The envelope peaks at $V_{max}$ = {{Vc*(1+m)|V}} and dips to $V_{min}$ = {{Vc*(1-m)|V}}.
$m = \frac{V_{max} - V_{min}}{V_{max} + V_{min}}$ = ({{Vc*(1+m)}} − {{Vc*(1-m)}}) / ({{Vc*(1+m)}} + {{Vc*(1-m)}}) = **{{m}}**.

steps.prompt: What happens when an AM transmitter is overmodulated ($m > 1$)?
options: The envelope is clipped, the audio distorts and extra sidebands disturb adjacent channels
The sidebands simply get stronger, which improves the range
steps.explanation: For $m > 1$ the envelope would have to go below zero, so the carrier is cut off during the troughs. The detected audio is then distorted, and the sharp corners create harmonics of the audio: sidebands far outside the channel (splatter).

steps.title: Sidebands
steps.body: Multiplying out the AM equation gives three sinusoids: the unchanged carrier and two **side frequencies** at $f_c - f_m$ (lower) and $f_c + f_m$ (upper), each with amplitude $mV_c/2$. A band of audio frequencies produces a lower and an upper **sideband**, so the AM signal is $2f_{m,max}$ wide. Shown: $f_c$ = 1 MHz, $f_m$ = 5 kHz, $m$ = 0.6.

steps.prompt: A {{fc|Hz|4}} carrier is amplitude-modulated by a {{fm|Hz}} tone. Which frequencies does the AM signal contain?
steps.explanation: Carrier plus two side frequencies $f_c \pm f_m$: {{fc-fm|Hz|5}} (lower), {{fc|Hz|5}} and {{fc+fm|Hz|5}} (upper). A varying amplitude is not a single frequency; mathematically it is exactly this sum of three sinusoids.

steps.prompt: An AM transmitter is modulated by audio up to {{fmax|Hz}}. What bandwidth does its signal occupy?
steps.explanation: The highest audio frequency produces the outermost side frequencies at $f_c \pm f_{m,max}$: $BW = 2f_{m,max}$ = 2 × {{fmax|Hz}} = **{{2*fmax|Hz}}**.

steps.prompt: Which spectrum belongs to an AM signal with $m$ = {{m}}, modulated by one tone ($f_c = 10f_m$)?
steps.explanation: A full-carrier AM signal has the carrier (amplitude $V_c$) plus two side frequencies of $mV_c/2$ = {{m/2}} $V_c$ each. Sidebands of $mV_c$ forget the factor ½, $m^2/4$ is the sideband **power** relative to the carrier, and the graph without a carrier is DSB-SC.

steps.prompt: In a full-carrier AM signal, all the information is in the sidebands; the carrier itself carries none.
steps.explanation: True. The carrier is the same with or without modulation; only the sidebands depend on the message. That is why suppressing the carrier (DSB-SC, SSB) saves so much power.

steps.prompt: An AM transmitter has a carrier power of {{Pc|W}} and is modulated to $m$ = {{m}}.

ask.prompt: Find the total transmitted power.
Find the power in one sideband.
Find the total power in both sidebands.

steps.prompt: The unmodulated carrier drives {{Ic|A}} rms into a {{R}} Ω antenna. The carrier is then modulated to $m$ = {{m}}.

ask.prompt: Find the modulated antenna current.
Find the total power delivered to the antenna.

steps.prompt: An RF ammeter in the antenna lead reads {{Ic|A}} with an unmodulated carrier and {{IT|A}} with modulation. Find the modulation index.
What percentage of the total transmitted power is in the two sidebands at $m$ = {{m}}?
steps.explanation: Sidebands: $P_cm^2/2$; total: $P_c(1 + m^2/2)$. Share: $\frac{m^2/2}{1 + m^2/2} = \frac{m^2}{2 + m^2}$ = **{{100*m^2/(2+m^2)||3}} %**. ({{100*m^2/2||3}} % is relative to the carrier, not the total; {{100*m^2/4||3}} % is one sideband relative to the carrier.)

steps.prompt: The carrier is {{Vc|V}} peak. Set the modulation index so that the envelope swings between $V_{max}$ = {{Vmax|V}} and $V_{min}$ = {{Vmin|V}} (orange dashed lines).
steps.explanation: $m = \frac{V_{max} - V_{min}}{V_{max} + V_{min}}$ = ({{Vmax}} − {{Vmin}}) / ({{Vmax}} + {{Vmin}}) = **{{mt}}**. Check: $V_m = mV_c$ = {{mt*Vc|V}} is half of $V_{max} - V_{min}$.

steps.prompt: An AM envelope on a scope peaks at $V_{max}$ = {{Vmax|V}} and dips to $V_{min}$ = {{Vmin|V}}.

ask.prompt: Find the modulation index.
Find the peak amplitude of the unmodulated carrier $V_c$.
ask.explanation: The envelope swings symmetrically around $V_c$: $V_c = (V_{max} + V_{min})/2$ = **{{(Vmax + Vmin)/2|V}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the peak amplitude of the modulating signal $V_m$.
ask.explanation: The envelope swings $\pm V_m$ around $V_c$: $V_m = (V_{max} - V_{min})/2$ = **{{(Vmax - Vmin)/2|V}}**.

steps.prompt: An AM transmitter delivers {{PT|W}} in total at $m$ = {{m}}. How much of this is carrier power?
steps.explanation: $P_c = \frac{P_T}{1 + m^2/2}$ = {{PT|W}} / {{1 + m^2/2||4}} = **{{PT/(1 + m^2/2)|W}}**; the sidebands get the remaining {{PT - PT/(1 + m^2/2)|W}}.

steps.prompt: Raising the modulation index of an AM transmitter from 0.5 to 1 doubles its total output power.
steps.explanation: False. $P_T = P_c(1 + m^2/2)$ goes from 1.125 $P_c$ to 1.5 $P_c$, only 33 % more. The **sideband** power, however, quadruples ($m^2$: 0.25 → 1).

steps.title: Suppressed-carrier signals
steps.body: DSB-SC drops the carrier; SSB also drops one sideband, so it needs half the bandwidth and every watt carries information. An SSB signal's power is rated at the envelope peak: the **peak envelope power**, with $V_p$ the peak of the envelope across the load $R$.

steps.prompt: A 100 %-modulated AM transmitter has a carrier power of {{Pc|W}}. An SSB transmitter puts all its power into one sideband.

ask.prompt: Which SSB output power gives the same power in one sideband as the AM transmitter?
ask.explanation: AM at $m = 1$: $P_{SB} = P_cm^2/4$ = {{Pc|W}}/4 = {{Pc/4|W}} per sideband. An SSB transmitter of **{{Pc/4|W}}** puts exactly this into its single sideband.

ask.prompt: How many times larger is the total AM power than this SSB power?
ask.explanation: AM total: $P_c(1 + 1/2)$ = {{1.5*Pc|W}}. SSB: {{Pc/4|W}}. Ratio: **6**, for any carrier power. The carrier and the second sideband are pure overhead. (Against the carrier power alone the ratio is 4, the often-quoted 4:1 power advantage of SSB.)

steps.prompt: On voice peaks an SSB transmitter produces {{Vpp}} V peak-to-peak across a {{R}} Ω antenna. What is its PEP?
An SSB transmitter is tested with two equal audio tones. Each tone on its own would deliver {{Pt|W}} to the antenna.

ask.prompt: What is the peak envelope power with both tones?
ask.explanation: The two RF tones drift in and out of phase. At the envelope peak their amplitudes add ($2V$), and power goes with amplitude squared: PEP = 4 × {{Pt|W}} = **{{4*Pt|W}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the average output power with both tones?
ask.explanation: Two different frequencies: their average powers simply add, 2 × {{Pt|W}} = **{{2*Pt|W}}**. So for a two-tone test PEP = 2 × $P_{avg}$.

steps.title: Choosing the detector RC
steps.body: In the diode detector, $C$ charges to each carrier peak and discharges through $R$. To smooth the carrier, $RC$ must span many carrier periods. To follow the envelope where it falls fastest, it must not exceed the limit below; otherwise the output lags behind in straight sloping lines (**diagonal clipping**). Use the highest $f_m$ and the highest $m$.

steps.prompt: An envelope detector with $R$ = {{R|Ω}} must handle audio up to {{fm|Hz}} at modulation indices up to {{m}}.

ask.prompt: What is the largest time constant $RC$ that avoids diagonal clipping?
What is the largest capacitor $C$ that avoids diagonal clipping?

steps.prompt: Set $RC$ for an AM signal with $m$ = {{m}} (here $f_c = 40f_m$): at least 4 carrier periods for low ripple, but without diagonal clipping.
steps.explanation: Ripple: $RC \geq 4T_c = 4T_m/40$ = 0.1 $T_m$. Clipping: $RC \leq \frac{\sqrt{1 - m^2}}{2\pi f_m m}$ = √(1 − {{m}}²)/(2π × {{m}}) $T_m$ = {{lim0||3}} $T_m$. Any value in between works. With the real ratio $f_c/f_m \approx 100$ there is far more room.

steps.prompt: The output of an AM diode detector follows the envelope at low audio frequencies, but at high audio frequencies it falls in straight sloping lines after each envelope peak. What is wrong?
options: The detector time constant $RC$ is too long
The detector time constant $RC$ is too short
The carrier frequency is too high
The diode is connected the wrong way round
steps.explanation: This is diagonal clipping: $C$ discharges through $R$ more slowly than the envelope falls. Reduce $RC$ to at most $\sqrt{1 - m^2}/(2\pi f_m m)$. Too short an $RC$ would show as carrier ripple instead; a reversed diode only inverts the output.

steps.prompt: Match each signal to its characteristic.
steps.explanation: Only full-carrier AM ($m \leq 1$) has an envelope that copies the message. DSB-SC is $x(t)\cos\omega_ct$: where $x(t)$ changes sign the carrier phase flips 180°. SSB with one tone is just a single sine at $f_c + f_m$ (or $f_c - f_m$). VSB was used for analog TV video, where a full second sideband would waste spectrum but a sharp cut would distort low frequencies.

steps.prompt: Order the stages of a filter-method SSB transmitter, from microphone to antenna.
steps.explanation: The balanced modulator makes DSB-SC at a fixed, convenient frequency where a steep crystal filter can remove one sideband. A mixer then moves the SSB signal to the operating frequency, and a **linear** amplifier boosts it (a class C stage would distort the varying envelope).

steps.prompt: A mediumwave transmitter has a carrier power of {{Pc|W}} into a {{R}} Ω antenna and is modulated to $m$ = {{m}}.

ask.prompt: Find the antenna current without modulation.
Find the antenna current with modulation.

steps.prompt: The antenna current of an AM transmitter ({{R}} Ω antenna) rises from {{Ic|A}} to {{IT|A}} when it is modulated. How much power is in each sideband?
steps.explanation: Carrier: $P_c = I_c^2R$ = {{Pc|W}}. Total: $P_T = I_T^2R$ = {{IT^2*R|W}}. The difference {{(IT^2 - Ic^2)*R|W}} is in the two sidebands, so each has **{{(IT^2 - Ic^2)*R/2|W}}**. (Via the index: $m$ = {{mm||3}}, $P_cm^2/4$ gives the same.)

steps.prompt: A station transmits AM at an average $m$ = {{m}}. It is replaced by an SSB transmitter that delivers the same power in one sideband. What percentage of the AM transmitter's total power is saved?
A filter-method SSB transmitter makes DSB-SC at {{fc|Hz}} from speech of {{fl|Hz}} to {{fh|Hz}}. The sideband filter must pass the upper sideband and suppress the lower one.

ask.prompt: How wide is the gap between the two sidebands?
ask.explanation: The LSB ends at $f_c - f_l$ and the USB starts at $f_c + f_l$: the gap is $2f_l$ = **{{2*fl|Hz}}**. The filter must go from pass to stop within this gap; the lack of low audio frequencies is what makes SSB filters possible.

ask.prompt: The filter's −6 dB passband exactly covers the USB, and its skirts are symmetric. What is the largest shape factor (−60 dB / −6 dB) that still suppresses the whole LSB by 60 dB?
ask.explanation: Passband: $f_c + f_l$ to $f_c + f_h$, width {{fh-fl|Hz}}, centre $f_c$ + {{(fl+fh)/2|Hz}}. The −60 dB band may reach down to the top of the LSB at $f_c - f_l$, i.e. {{(fl+fh)/2 + fl|Hz}} below the centre, so it may be 2 × {{(fl+fh)/2 + fl|Hz}} = {{3*fl + fh|Hz}} wide. $SF \leq$ {{3*fl + fh|Hz}} / {{fh - fl|Hz}} = **{{(3*fl + fh)/(fh - fl)||3}}**: only a crystal filter achieves this.

steps.prompt: A receiver with a 455 kHz IF has a diode detector with $R$ = {{R|Ω}}. Audio reaches {{fm|Hz}} and the modulation peaks at $m$ = {{m}}.

ask.prompt: Find the largest capacitor that avoids diagonal clipping.
How many IF carrier periods does this largest $RC$ span?
ask.explanation: $RC_{max}$ = $\frac{\sqrt{1 - m^2}}{2\pi f_m m}$ = {{tau|s}}; one IF period is 1/455 kHz = 2.2 µs. Ratio: **{{tau*455e3||3}}** periods, so the carrier ripple is small while the envelope is still followed.

steps.prompt: A synchronous detector demodulates DSB-SC, but its local carrier has a phase error of {{phi}}°. The output amplitude is proportional to $\cos\varphi$.

ask.prompt: What percentage of the ideal output amplitude remains?
ask.explanation: $x(t)\cos\omega_ct \cdot \cos(\omega_ct + \varphi)$ contains $\tfrac{1}{2}x(t)\cos\varphi$ after the low-pass filter: cos {{phi}}° = **{{100*cos(rad(phi))||3}} %**. At 90° the output vanishes, which is why the carrier must be recovered in phase.

ask.prompt: By how many dB does the output drop?
ask.explanation: Amplitude ratio cos {{phi}}° = {{cos(rad(phi))||3}}; in dB: −20 log({{cos(rad(phi))||3}}) = **{{-20*log10(cos(rad(phi)))||3}} dB** lower.

steps.prompt: In a phasing SSB generator one balanced modulator gets $\cos\omega_mt$ and $\cos\omega_ct$, the other $\sin\omega_mt$ and $\sin\omega_ct$. The outputs are **subtracted**. With $f_c$ = {{fc|Hz}} and $f_m$ = {{fm|Hz}}, what is left?
steps.explanation: $\cos A\cos B - \sin A\sin B = \cos(A + B)$: the difference frequencies cancel and only the upper sideband $f_c + f_m$ = **{{fc+fm|Hz|6}}** remains. Adding the outputs instead gives $\cos(A - B)$, the lower sideband.

steps.prompt: Each trace shows a carrier modulated by one tone. Which one is a DSB-SC signal?
steps.explanation: DSB-SC is $x(t)\sin\omega_ct$: its envelope is $|x(t)|$, touching zero twice per tone period, with a phase reversal at each zero. The full-carrier AM traces ($m$ = 0.5 and $m$ = 1) keep their envelope above zero (at $m$ = 1 it just touches zero once per period), and the constant sine is SSB.

steps.prompt: A DSB-SC signal modulated by a 1 kHz tone is fed to an ordinary envelope detector. What comes out?
options: A distorted signal $|x(t)|$ with its main component at 2 kHz
Nothing at all, since there is no carrier
A 1 kHz tone at half the amplitude
steps.explanation: The envelope of $x(t)\cos\omega_ct$ is $|x(t)|$: for a tone a full-wave rectified sine, whose fundamental is at twice the tone frequency. DSB-SC needs synchronous detection with a re-inserted carrier.
